To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the maternal immune system is altered in a unique way during pregnancy to tolerate the developing fetus, and that prenatal infections can exploit the maternal immune system in a way that can lead to adverse pregnancy outcomes.

maternal Treg cells are required for the establishment and maintenance of maternal tolerance of fetal antigens and that Treg cells are essential to prevent maternal immune rejection of the fetus and the associated pregnancy complications.
maternal CD4 T cell regulatory subsets play a central role in pregnancy and that pathogens with predisposition for prenatal infection can exploit this immunological milieu for pathogenesis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of Treg cells in pregnancy and prenatal infections.
the role of maternal Tregs in prenatal infection susceptibility and how this immune subset may become hijacked by prenatal pathogens to cause infection-induced pregnancy complications.
the role of maternal Tregs in the immune pathogenesis associated with prenatal infections.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the role of maternal Tregs in prenatal infection pathogenesis has only begun to be appreciated.
maternal Tregs are necessary for fetal survival.
maternal Tregs play a central role in the immune pathogenesis and pathophysiology of prenatal infection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
maternal regulatory T cells play a critical role in the immune homeostasis of pregnancy.
prenatal infection susceptibility is a double-edged sword that can be manipulated by the pathogen to its advantage, and this can be detrimental to the fetus.
the immune pathogenesis and pathophysiological outcomes of prenatal infection are dictated by maternal Treg-mediated suppression.
The main takeaway from our work is that
prenatal infection is an immune pathogenetic process that may be modulated by the maternal Treg response.
prenatal infection susceptibility and pregnancy complications can be attributed to a failure to expand maternal Treg suppressive function.
prenatal infections can have a profound influence on maternal immune responses that can either protect the fetus from infection or compromise fetal tolerance.
